paper_metadata.title: Processing, Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of the CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy

evidence.quote: namely the single-phase, face-centered cubic alloy CrMnFeCoNi, with emphasis on its excellent damage tolerance (strength with toughness) in the temperature range from room temperature down to liquid nitrogen temperature.
The alloy had been induction melted in an alumina crucible and exhibited significant dendritic segregation
A comparable size button of this alloy that was subsequently arc-melted in 2008 at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) on a water-cooled copper hearth exhibited less severe segregation (Fig. 1)
many larger ingots weighing approximately 500 g (≈25 mm in diameter and 127 mm long) were produced at ORNL by arc melting and drop casting.
it was possible to homogenize them by annealing at 1000–1200°C for 24–48 h.
even larger ingots (40 mm in diameter) have been successfully homogenized at the Ruhr University in Bochum by annealing at 1200°C for 48 h.

During multi-pass rolling at 1000°C to a total reduction in thickness of ≈90%, the alloy undergoes dynamic recrystallization resulting in an equiaxed microstructure with ≈30 μm grains containing numerous twins
Extensive deformation by multi-pass rolling at room temperature is possible, with total reductions in thickness of as much as 90% without the need for any intermediate anneals.

High degrees of deformation are also possible by multi-step swaging at room temperature without intermediate annealing, resulting in a reduction of diameter from 40 mm to 16.5 mm (i.e., area reduction of ≈80%).

Cryogenic rolling at 77 K has also been performed with the rolls and sheet immersed in liquid nitrogen to allow for isothermal conditions. Total reductions in thickness of up to 80% were possible without intermediate anneals.
After rolling at room temperature recrystallization by annealing at elevated temperatures (>800°C) results in almost perfectly equiaxed single-phase grains containing numerous annealing twins

After severe plastic deformation by HPT (strains of approximately 5000%), grain size was significantly reduced, down into the nanoscale (≈50 nm), but the cast and homogenized HEA retained its true solid solution state down to the atomic scale
subsequent annealing at 450°C resulted in nanoscale precipitation in the HEA matrix: first to appear were NiMn and Cr, followed at longer times by FeCo.
